topic: World Health Organization Surgical Safety Checklist Implementation Phases
stem: A hospital quality improvement initiative reviews adverse surgical events and near-misses over a 3-year period. The analysis reveals two wrong-site surgeries (an incorrect toe amputation and a left-sided instead of right-sided arthroscopy) and multiple near-miss retained surgical sponges. In response, the health system mandates rigorous adherence to the WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION (WHO) SURGICAL SAFETY CHECKLIST across all operating rooms. Which of the following represents the correct three distinct procedural phases and timing of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist?

options.text: Pre-op check (in the preoperative holding area), Incision pause (after skin incision), and Recovery sign-off (in the PACU)
options.explanation: The Time-out MUST occur BEFORE skin incision (not after), and Sign-out must occur BEFORE leaving the operating room.

options.text: Anesthesia induction, Surgical incision, and Post-anesthesia discharge to the general medical floor
options.explanation: These are standard operative milestones, not the structured three-phase safety verification checklist.

options.text: Sign-in (before induction of anesthesia), Time-out (before skin incision), and Sign-out (before the patient leaves the operating room)
options.explanation: The WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION (WHO) SURGICAL SAFETY CHECKLIST is a global patient safety tool proven in landmark prospective multicenter trials (Haynes et al., NEJM 2009) to REDUCE MAJOR SURGICAL COMPLICATIONS BY >35% AND INPATIENT SURGICAL MORTALITY BY >45%: (1) THREE RIGID PROCEDURAL PHASES: (a) SIGN-IN (BEFORE INDUCTION OF ANESTHESIA): Conducted with the patient, nurse, and anesthetist. Verifies: patient identity, surgical procedure, anatomical site marking, informed consent, anesthesia safety check, pulse oximeter on patient, and evaluation of difficult airway/aspiration risk and blood loss risk (>500 mL); (b) TIME-OUT (BEFORE SKIN INCISION): Conducted with the entire surgical team (surgeon, anesthetist, nurses). Brief pause to verbally confirm: all team members introduced by name and role, patient identity, surgical procedure and exact operative site, display of essential imaging, administration of prophylactic antibiotics within 60 minutes prior to incision, and anticipated critical steps/operative duration; and (c) SIGN-OUT (BEFORE THE PATIENT LEAVES THE OR): Conducted with nurse, surgeon, and anesthetist. Verbally confirms: name of procedure recorded, needle/sponge/instrument counts are correct, specimen labeling, and key recovery and management concerns; and (2) Eliminates wrong-site surgery and retained items.

options.text: Sterility check (during scrub), Instrument count (during fascial closure), and Pathology drop-off (the next morning)
options.explanation: Pathology drop-off occurs post-procedure; checklist phases are strictly timed around induction, incision, and leaving the room.

options.text: Universal protocol, Patient identification, and Informed consent signing prior to hospital admission
options.explanation: Informed consent is obtained prior to surgery; the three live intraoperative WHO checklist phases are Sign-in, Time-out, and Sign-out.

subject: Geriatrics
topic: Hospital Inpatient Fall Prevention Multicomponent Interventions
stem: An 82-year-old woman with mild vascular dementia, osteoporosis, and osteoarthritis of the knees is admitted to the general medicine hospitalist service for treatment of acute pyelonephritis. On admission, nursing fall risk assessment using the Morse Fall Scale classifies her as high risk for inpatient falls (prior fall at home 3 weeks ago, impaired gait, unfamiliar surroundings). On hospital night 1, she attempts to get out of bed unassisted to use the bathroom, trips over her intravenous tubing, and falls to the floor, sustaining a non-displaced right distal radius fracture. The hospital quality improvement team reviews her care to implement a hospital-wide inpatient fall prevention protocol. Which of the following represents the most evidence-based, guideline-directed multicomponent strategy to prevent inpatient falls and related injuries in hospitalized older adults?

options.text: Application of bilateral soft wrist restraints and vest restraints whenever the patient is unattended in bed
options.explanation: Physical restraints do not prevent falls or injuries, cause severe psychological trauma and strangulation, and are strictly contraindicated for routine fall prevention.

options.text: Administration of scheduled oral lorazepam 1 mg at bedtime to ensure the patient remains asleep and does not exit the bed
options.explanation: Sedatives and benzodiazepines directly impair coordination, cause ataxia, worsen delirium, and dramatically increase nighttime fall and fracture rates.

options.text: Bedside placement of four raised full-length bed rails locked in the upright position at all times
options.explanation: Full-length side rails act as an obstacle that confused patients attempt to climb over, causing falls from greater heights with more severe head injuries.

options.text: A multifactorial bundle comprising purposeful hourly nursing rounds, scheduled assisted toileting, low beds with non-skid footwear, bed alarms, assistive devices within reach, and deprescribing sedatives, while strictly avoiding physical restraints
options.explanation: INPATIENT FALLS are the most common adverse event reported in hospitalized older adults, resulting in hip fractures, intracranial hemorrhage, and prolonged hospital stays. Guidelines from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), American Geriatrics Society (AGS), and CDC establish that: (1) EFFECTIVE MULTIFACTORIAL FALL PREVENTION BUNDLES: Successful fall prevention requires a combination of simultaneous interventions: (a) PURPOSEFUL HOURLY ROUNDING (the '4 Ps': Pain, Position, Potty, Possessions): Actively addressing pain, repositioning, offering assisted toileting, and ensuring call lights and glasses are within reach; (b) SCHEDULED ASSISTED TOILETING: Unassisted attempts to reach the bathroom account for >50% of inpatient falls; (c) ENVIRONMENTAL SAFETY: Low-height beds, floor mats, non-skid socks, clear walking paths free of IV tubing, and bed-exit alarms; and (d) MEDICATION REVIEW: Deprescribing high-risk fall-inducing medications (sedative-hypnotics, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines); and (2) PHYSICAL RESTRAINTS DO NOT PREVENT FALLS: Clinical trials conclusively prove that physical restraints (wrist restraints, vest restraints) DO NOT REDUCE FALLS OR FRACTURES. In fact, restraints INCREASE FALL-RELATED INJURIES (from entangling and struggling), accelerate functional decline, and triple delirium rates.

options.explanation: Enforced bed rest causes rapid muscle deconditioning, deep vein thrombosis, and CAUTIs, worsening post-discharge fall rates.

topic: Hospital-Acquired Pressure Injury Prevention Braden Scale and Repositioning
stem: A 76-year-old man who suffered an acute ischemic stroke resulting in dense right-sided hemiplegia and global aphasia is admitted to the neurological step-down unit. He is bedbound, incontinent of bowel and bladder, and unable to reposition himself in bed. Physical examination reveals an alert but non-verbal man with flaccid right extremities. Skin examination on admission reveals intact, blanchable erythema over the sacrum without skin breakdown (Stage 1 pressure injury). Nutritional assessment demonstrates severe protein-calorie malnutrition (serum albumin 2.4 g/dL). His calculated BRADEN SCALE score is 11 (high risk for severe pressure ulcer development; scale ranges from 6 to 23, with scores <= 12 indicating high risk). Which of the following is the most effective evidence-based hospital prevention bundle recommended by the National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP) to prevent pressure injury progression and hospital-acquired pressure injuries (HAPIs)?

options.text: Maintaining the patient continuously in a flat supine position without turning to prevent friction and shearing forces
options.explanation: Continuous supine positioning produces uninterrupted ischemic necrosis over the sacrum and heels, accelerating rapid ulcer ulceration into deep muscle.

options.text: Vigorous, aggressive manual massage over bony prominences with alcohol rub every 4 hours to stimulate cutaneous blood flow
options.explanation: Massaging over bony prominences causes deep capillary shearing, microvascular thrombosis, and severe soft tissue necrosis and is strictly contraindicated.

options.text: Application of a rigid plastic cervical collar and sandbags around the pelvic girdle to restrict all spontaneous patient movement
options.explanation: Immobilizing a patient multiplies continuous interface pressure over bony prominences, accelerating deep tissue injury.

options.text: Limiting body repositioning to once every 12 hours provided a standard hospital vinyl mattress is used
options.explanation: Repositioning every 12 hours causes sustained tissue ischemia exceeding 10 hours, guaranteeing full-thickness tissue breakdown.

options.text: A multimodal prevention protocol comprising scheduled body repositioning every 2 hours, pressure-redistributing dynamic air or foam mattress surfaces, barrier creams for moisture management, and high-protein nutritional supplementation
options.explanation: HOSPITAL-ACQUIRED PRESSURE INJURIES (HAPIs / decubitus ulcers) are localized damage to the skin and underlying soft tissue, usually over a bony prominence (sacrum, ischium, greater trochanter, heels), resulting from intense or prolonged pressure in combination with shear. The National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP) and American College of Physicians (ACP) guidelines mandate an EVIDENCE-BASED PRESSURE INJURY PREVENTION BUNDLE for high-risk patients (Braden score <= 12): (1) FREQUENT REPOSITIONING: Scheduled manual repositioning AT LEAST EVERY 2 HOURS (in bed) or every 1 hour (in chair), using a 30-degree tilted side-lying position (avoiding direct 90-degree lateral pressure on the greater trochanter); (2) ADVANCED SUPPORT SURFACES: Use of specialized PRESSURE-REDISTRIBUTING SUPPORT SURFACES (dynamic alternating-pressure air mattresses or high-density foam overlays) to reduce interface pressure below capillary closing pressure (32 mm Hg); (3) MOISTURE MANAGEMENT: Prompt cleansing after incontinence, application of skin barrier creams/ointments (zinc oxide, dimethicone), and avoiding diaper occlusive traps; (4) OFF-LOADING HEELS: Complete heel floating using heel-suspension boots or pillows under calves; and (5) NUTRITIONAL OPTIMIZATION: High-protein oral or enteral supplements to support tissue healing and collagen synthesis.
